title: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

guide.summary: This unit extends energy and momentum to rotation: rotational kinetic energy, work done by torques, rolling without slipping, angular momentum of particles and rigid bodies, angular impulse, and conservation of angular momentum, including orbital motion.

sections.heading: Rotational energy and rolling
sections.body: Rotational kinetic energy K_rot = ½Iω². Work done by a torque: W = ∫τ dθ; the rotational work–energy theorem is W_net = ΔK_rot. Rolling without slipping: v_cm = ωR, a_cm = αR, and total kinetic energy K = ½Mv_cm² + ½I_cmω². Static friction acts at the contact point but does no work (the contact point is instantaneously at rest), so mechanical energy is conserved for objects rolling without slipping. Rolling down an incline from height h: v = √[2gh/(1 + I/MR²)]. Objects with smaller I/MR² (solid sphere 2/5 < disk 1/2 < hoop 1) reach the bottom faster, independent of mass and radius.

sections.heading: Angular momentum
sections.body: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = Iω. For a particle, L = r × p, with magnitude mvr sin θ = mv·(perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of motion); a particle moving in a straight line has constant angular momentum about any fixed point if no torque acts. Newton's second law for rotation: Στ = dL/dt; angular impulse ∫τ dt = ΔL.

sections.heading: Conservation of angular momentum
sections.body: If the net external torque on a system is zero, total angular momentum is conserved: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. A spinning skater pulling in her arms decreases I and increases ω; her kinetic energy increases because she does work pulling her arms in. When a particle collides with and sticks to a rotating or pivoted object, angular momentum about the pivot is conserved (the pivot force exerts no torque about the pivot), but kinetic energy is not, and linear momentum is generally not conserved because the pivot exerts an external force. For orbits, gravity exerts no torque about the planet's center, so the satellite's angular momentum is conserved (Kepler's second law: it moves faster closer in).

sections.heading: Worked example: rolling down an incline
sections.body: A solid sphere (I = (2/5)MR²) rolls without slipping down an incline of height h. Energy conservation gives Mgh = ½Mv² + ½(2/5)MR²(v/R)² = (7/10)Mv², so v = √(10gh/7). The acceleration along an incline of angle θ is a = (5/7)g sin θ. Static friction provides the torque for rolling but does no work, because the contact point is momentarily at rest.

sections.heading: Worked example: a collision with rotation
sections.body: A 0.10 kg ball moving at 10 m/s strikes and sticks to the end of a 2.0 kg rod of length 1.0 m pivoted at its other end. Angular momentum about the pivot is conserved: (0.10)(10)(1.0) = I_total ω, where I_total = (1/3)(2.0)(1.0)² + (0.10)(1.0)² ≈ 0.767 kg·m², so ω ≈ 1.30 rad/s. Linear momentum is not conserved because the pivot exerts an external force.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students forget to include rotational kinetic energy, use linear momentum conservation when a pivot exerts force, and confuse rolling with slipping.

sections.heading: Exam connection
sections.body: Expect questions comparing objects rolling down inclines, collisions with rotating rods, and angular momentum of particles moving in straight lines relative to a point.

sections.heading: Laboratory and experimental design
sections.body: To compare rolling objects, release a hoop, a disk, and a sphere from the same height on an incline and time their descent. The sphere arrives first, then the disk, then the hoop, regardless of mass and radius, because a smaller fraction of each one's kinetic energy is rotational.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body: K_rot = ½Iω²; rolling: v = ωR; L = Iω; L = r × p for particles; τ_net = dL/dt; L conserved when external torque is zero.

sections.heading: Derivation tips
sections.body: When deriving rolling results, include both translational and rotational kinetic energy and use the rolling condition v = ωR. For collisions with pivots, use angular momentum about the pivot, since the pivot force exerts no torque about that point.

sections.heading: Graph skills
sections.body: On an angular momentum-versus-time graph, the slope equals the net external torque, so a horizontal line means zero net torque. Graphs of rotational and translational kinetic energy for rolling objects show how energy divides between the two forms depending on rotational inertia.

keyTakeaways: K_rot = ½Iω²; rolling: K = ½Mv² + ½Iω².
Rolling without slipping: v = ωR; static friction does no work.
Smaller I/MR² → faster down an incline.
Pivoted collisions: conserve L about the pivot, not p or K.
commonMistakes: Ignoring rotational KE for rolling objects.
Conserving linear momentum in a collision with a pivoted object.
Thinking kinetic energy is conserved when a skater pulls in her arms.
Assuming heavier rolling objects arrive first.
Using the wrong distance for a particle's angular momentum (must be perpendicular distance).
examTips: Energy bar charts for rolling: include both translational and rotational KE.
For collisions with rods, compute L of the incoming particle about the pivot.
Rank rolling objects with the I/MR² coefficient.
For orbits, use angular momentum conservation for speed at different radii.
guide.cramSheet:
**Rotational KE:** ½Iω² · W = ∫τ dθ

**Rolling:** v = ωR · K = ½Mv² + ½Iω² · v = √(2gh/(1 + I/MR²)) · sphere > disk > hoop

**Angular momentum:** L = Iω · L = mvr⊥ · Στ = dL/dt

**Conservation:** Στ_ext = 0 → I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ · KE may change

**Pivoted collision:** conserve L about pivot only

**Orbits:** L conserved → faster when closer

vocab.definition: Kinetic energy due to rotation: ½Iω².
Rolling where the contact point is instantaneously at rest: v_cm = ωR.
L = Iω about a fixed axis.
L = r × p, magnitude mv times perpendicular distance.
The integral of torque over time, equal to the change in angular momentum.
With zero net external torque, a system's total angular momentum is constant.
A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, a consequence of angular momentum conservation.
Perpendicular distance from the axis to a particle's line of motion.
Kinetic energy of the center of mass: ½Mv_cm².
Friction at the contact point that enables rolling but does no work if there's no slipping.
Net work by torques equals the change in rotational kinetic energy.

practice.stem: A solid disk (I = ½MR²) rolls without slipping at speed v. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
practice.explanation: K_rot = ½(½MR²)(v/R)² = ¼Mv²; total = ¾Mv²; ratio = 1/3.

practice.stem: A spinning ice skater pulls her arms in, reducing her rotational inertia from 4.0 kg·m² to 1.6 kg·m². Her initial angular speed was 2.0 rad/s. What is her final angular speed?
A solid sphere, a solid cylinder, and a hoop are released from rest at the top of the same incline and roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
practice.explanation: Smallest I/MR² (2/5) puts the largest share of energy into translation.

practice.stem: A 2.0 kg particle moves in a straight line at 3.0 m/s. Its line of motion passes 4.0 m from point O at its closest. What is its angular momentum about O?

choices.text: It changes as the particle moves.

practice.explanation: L = mv r⊥ = 2(3)(4) = 24 kg·m²/s, constant along the line.

distractors.D: r sin θ stays equal to the perpendicular distance.

practice.stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of vertical height 1.4 m. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
In the skater example (I from 4.0 to 1.6 kg·m², ω from 2.0 to 5.0 rad/s), how does her rotational kinetic energy change?

choices.text: It increases from 8.0 J to 20 J because she does work pulling her arms in.
It increases because angular momentum increases.

practice.explanation: K = ½Iω²: ½(4)(4) = 8 J → ½(1.6)(25) = 20 J. Angular momentum stays constant.

practice.stem: A merry-go-round (I = 200 kg·m²) spins at 1.0 rad/s. A 25 kg child, initially at rest, steps on at the rim 2.0 m from the axis. What is the new angular speed?

distractors.C: Uses the child's I as 25 kg·m².

practice.stem: A constant 4.0 N·m torque acts on a wheel through 10 revolutions starting from rest. How much rotational kinetic energy does the wheel gain?
Which statement about friction on a ball rolling without slipping down an incline is correct?

choices.text: Static friction acts and provides the torque for angular acceleration, but does no work.

practice.explanation: The contact point is instantaneously at rest, so static friction does no work.

practice.stem: A comet's distance from the Sun at its closest point is one-tenth its distance at its farthest point. How does its speed at closest approach compare with its speed at farthest point?
practice.explanation: At both points, velocity ⟂ radius: mv₁r₁ = mv₂r₂.

practice.stem: A 1.0 kg uniform rod 1.0 m long pivots about its center on a frictionless horizontal surface. A 0.10 kg lump of putty moving at 10 m/s perpendicular to the rod sticks to one end. What is the angular speed afterward?
In the putty–rod collision (pivot at center), which quantities are conserved for the putty-rod system?

choices.text: Linear momentum, angular momentum, and kinetic energy
Angular momentum about the pivot only

practice.explanation: The pivot exerts an external force (so p isn't conserved) but no torque about itself; the sticking collision is inelastic.

practice.stem: A hollow sphere (I = (2/3)MR²) and a solid sphere roll without slipping up the same incline with the same initial center-of-mass speed. Which travels farther up the incline?
practice.explanation: Same v gives the hollow sphere more total KE (more rotational energy), which converts to more height.

practice.stem: A constant torque of 3.0 N·m acts for 4.0 s on a flywheel initially spinning at 5.0 rad/s with I = 2.0 kg·m², in the direction of rotation. What is the final angular speed?

practice.prompt: Several round objects, each with mass M, radius R, and rotational inertia I = βMR² (β is a number between 0 and 1), are released from rest at height h on an incline and roll without slipping.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) energy bar charts for the object–Earth system at the top and at the bottom of the incline, showing gravitational potential, translational kinetic, and rotational kinetic energy.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Starting from conservation of energy, derive the speed of an object at the bottom in terms of β, g, and h.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) a graph of v² at the bottom as a function of β for 0 ≤ β ≤ 1.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain how your bar charts, expression, and graph are consistent with each other, and why mass and radius don't affect the result.

rubric.description: U_g = 0; K_trans and K_rot sum to the original U_g; K_rot is a fraction β of K_trans.
Larger β puts a larger share of energy into rotation, leaving less for translation.
1 + β in denominator produces the decreasing graph.
M cancels from every term, and R cancels via ω = v/R, so only β matters.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. At the top, the bar chart shows only gravitational potential energy (U_g). At the bottom, U_g is zero, and the energy is split between translational kinetic energy and rotational kinetic energy, whose bars together equal the original U_g bar; the rotational bar is β times the translational bar.

B. Energy is conserved because static friction does no work: Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω². Rolling without slipping gives ω = v/R, and I = βMR², so ½Iω² = ½βMR²(v²/R²) = ½βMv². Then Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + β), and v = √[2gh/(1 + β)].

C. The graph of v² vs. β starts at 2gh when β = 0 and decreases along a concave-up curve to gh at β = 1.

D. The bar charts show that the same total energy is shared between translation and rotation; as β increases, the rotational share grows, leaving less for translation. That's why 1 + β is in the denominator of the expression, producing the decreasing graph. Mass cancels because both U_g and each kinetic energy term are proportional to M, and the radius cancels because the rotational energy depends on R² in I and on 1/R² in ω², so only the shape factor β determines the speed.
